subcommands.description:
Prints the value in effect, and says whether it comes from the file or from the
built-in default. That difference is the useful part: a setting absent from the
file behaves as the default today and would change if the default ever did.

subcommands.name: path

subcommands.description: The commented file ratline ships, with every default and the reasoning behind it.

subcommands.name: set

subcommands.description:
Edits the file in place, preserving its comments, then validates the result. If
the change would produce a file that does not load, the previous one is put back
and the error names the setting.

subcommands.name: show
subcommands.summary: Show the settings in effect

subcommands.description:

for a path or an address is usually not what anybody wants.

commands.summary: Provision MongoDB, MySQL or Redis databases and users
commands.description:
Creates databases and least-privilege users on a MongoDB server, and writes the
connection string into a site's .env so the application picks it up on restart.

flags.name: engine
flags.usage: Database engine: mongo, mysql or redis

examples: ratline db create shop --owner acme --attach shop.example.com
ratline db user add reports --database shop --role read
ratline db create shop --engine mysql --owner acme --attach shop.example.com

subcommands.name: access
subcommands.summary: Control which addresses can reach this host's MongoDB
subcommands.description:
Manages remote access to the MongoDB server `ratline db install` set up. By
default that server listens only on localhost. Allowing an address adds a ufw rule
admitting it to port 27017 and — on the first address — reconfigures mongod to
listen on all interfaces, in that order: the firewall stands guard before the
door opens. Revoking the last address puts mongod back on localhost only.
examples: ratline db access allow 203.0.113.19          # one machine
ratline db access allow 10.8.0.0/24 --note vpn # a network

subcommands.name: allow
subcommands.summary: Let an address or network reach MongoDB
subcommands.description:
Adds a ufw rule admitting the address to port 27017. The first allowed address
also reconfigures mongod to listen beyond localhost and restarts it — firewall
rule first, wider bind second, and the outcome is verified against the running
server: it must still enforce authorization, and it must actually be listening
where the config says.

flags.name: note
flags.usage: A word on whose address this is, shown in the list

subcommands.name: list
subcommands.summary: Show who can reach this host's MongoDB
subcommands.description:
Shows the allowed addresses, what mongod is bound to, and whether the firewall
is still standing guard — together, because each is meaningless without the
others.

subcommands.name: revoke
subcommands.summary: Stop an address reaching MongoDB
subcommands.description:
Deletes the ufw rule an allow created. Revoking the last allowed address also
puts mongod back to listening on localhost only, restarts it, and verifies both
facts against the running server.

subcommands.name: connect
subcommands.summary: Point ratline at a MongoDB server and turn provisioning on
subcommands.description:
Stores the admin connection string, turns on features.db_provisioning, and proves
the credentials work before committing either. If the server cannot be reached, or
rejects them, nothing is left behind.

notes: Every mutating command accepts --dry-run, which writes nothing at any layer. Run it first and read the plan.
Exit codes are a contract; branch on them rather than on message text.
Secrets are never accepted as flag values. --stdin, or a prompt on a terminal.
Commands are safe to run twice: re-running one that has already been applied reports what exists rather than failing.
